## Example 7.5(a) {#ss7-example-7-5-a .lim-lesson }

Consider the geometric series:

$$\sin x+\sin^2x+\sin^3x+\cdots.$$

**(a)** Show that, for a limiting sum to exist, we must have $x\ne\dfrac{n\pi}{2}$ for **odd** values of $n$.

::: {.fragment data-fragment-index="0"}

$$r=\sin x,\qquad |\sin x|<1$$

:::

::: {.fragment data-fragment-index="1"}

$$\sin x\ne\pm1\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad x\ne\frac{n\pi}{2}\quad(n\text{ odd})$$

:::

<p class="booklet-cue">Booklet p. 46 · Example 7.5(a)</p>

::: notes

Treat x as a fixed real parameter and angles in radians. Each term is obtained by multiplying by sin x. At sin x=0 all terms are zero and the sum is 0, so these values are included. Do not divide successive terms at these values. At sin x=1 the partial sums grow; at sin x=−1 they alternate −1,0. Hence exclude exactly odd multiples of π/2, equivalently π/2+kπ for k integer. Click 1 identifies the multiplier and condition. Click 2 records the excluded x-values.

:::
